Long-Context Foundation Models

Slim Foundation Models for Latency-Critical Recommendation Serving

Danyal Aftab Affiliation: Technological University Dublin Affiliation: Dublin, Ireland Email: Danyal.Aftab@TUDublin.ie    Anas Zafar Affiliation: National University of Computer and Emerging Science Affiliation: Karachi, Pakistan Email: anaszafar98@gmail.com    Assadig Abakr Affiliation: Technological University Dublin Affiliation: Dublin, Ireland Email: D23125151@mytudublin.ie    Steven Davy Affiliation: Technological University Dublin Affiliation: Dublin, Ireland Email: Steven.Davy@TUDublin.ie
Abstract

Click-through rate (CTR) prediction is a core component of recommendation and advertising systems. Large language models (LLMs) offer rich semantic priors that improve prediction quality, particularly in cold-start and long-tail settings. Injecting a full-scale LLM into a CTR pipeline is, however, prohibitively expensive at inference time: existing LLM-enhanced CTR methods avoid this cost by caching LLM outputs offline rather than serving the LLM online. We propose a resource-efficient pipeline, SlimFM, that makes online LLM-based semantic modeling practical: (1) dependency-aware structured pruning compresses LLaMA3-8B by 44% to a 4.5B-parameter backbone; (2) LoRA-based field-aware fine-tuning trains the pruned model to produce discriminative field-level semantic embeddings from lightweight textual prompts; (3) a semantic-guided fusion module injects these embeddings into the feature interactions of a conventional CTR model. Across four datasets and six CTR backbones, SlimFM retains over 99% of uncompressed-model accuracy while reducing inference latency by up to 3.4×3.4\times relative to existing LLM-enhanced baselines.

1 Introduction

CTR prediction is a critical component in recommender systems and digital advertising (Guo et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2018; Gligorijevic et al., 2019). Large language models can enrich this pipeline with semantic and world knowledge that ID-based models lack, particularly for cold-start items and long-tail users (Xi et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Qiu et al., 2024). The primary obstacle is computational cost: modern CTR backbones comprise on the order of 1–10M parameters, while contemporary LLMs such as LLaMA3-8B comprise 8B or more, making inference with a complete LLM infeasible under real-time serving constraints. Prior LLM-enhanced CTR methods therefore pre-compute and cache LLM outputs offline, serving only the CTR model online. Representative methods such as KAR (Xi et al., 2024), LLM-CF (Sun et al., 2024), CTRL (Li et al., 2023), and EASE (Qiu et al., 2024) incur, on average, over 290 times higher computational cost than standard CTR baselines (Cui et al., 2025). This approach transfers the computational burden from online serving to offline preprocessing rather than eliminating it; moreover, cached outputs must be regenerated whenever the item or feature catalog changes. This work investigates whether structured pruning of the LLM, combined with parameter-efficient fine-tuning, can compress the backbone sufficiently to enable online serving within the same request path as the CTR model, without significant degradation in semantic quality.

Contributions.

  • •

    A dependency-aware structured pruning procedure that compresses LLaMA3-8B to a 4.5B-parameter backbone (44% smaller) while preserving the representational capacity needed for downstream semantic-embedding extraction.

  • •

    Field-aware LoRA-based fine-tuning and a semantic-guided fusion mechanism together enable a pruned LLM to be served online rather than cached offline inside a latency-critical CTR pipeline.

  • •

    Across four datasets ×\times six CTR backbones, 44% parameter reduction retains >>99% of baseline accuracy at up to 3.4×3.4\times lower inference latency than existing LLM-enhanced CTR baselines.

2 Method

Figure 1 summarizes the three stages of SlimFM.

Structured Model Pruning.

Following DepGraph (Fang et al., 2023) and LLM-Pruner (Ma et al., 2023), we build a dependency graph over the attention and feed-forward parameters of LLaMA3-8B (Dubey et al., 2024), grouping structurally coupled parameters into prunable units 𝒢={Pk}k=1N\mathcal{G}=\{P_{k}\}_{k=1}^{N}. The importance of each group is estimated via a Taylor expansion of the next-token prediction loss:

I𝒢=∑k=1N|∂ℒ∂Pk⊤​Pk−12​Pk⊤​H​Pk|,I_{\mathcal{G}}=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\left|\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial P_{k}}^{\!\top}P_{k}-\tfrac{1}{2}P_{k}^{\top}HP_{k}\right|, (1)

where HH is the Hessian. Groups with the lowest I𝒢I_{\mathcal{G}} are removed until a target sparsity is reached, yielding a 4.5B-parameter backbone.

Field-Aware Semantic Learning.

We adapt the pruned LLM to the CTR domain via a field-identification task, using structured prompts that list the MM candidate field names (e.g., classifying ‘Black Rose’ as field MovieID). For a feature value vv from field ff, the LLM encodes the prompt into a query representation hh and each candidate field name into embeddings {efj}j=1M\{e_{f_{j}}\}_{j=1}^{M}. We train the model using an InfoNCE-style contrastive loss:

ℒfield=−log⁡exp⁡(h⋅ef+/τ)∑j=1Mexp⁡(h⋅efj/τ),\mathcal{L}_{\text{field}}=-\log\frac{\exp(h\cdot e_{f^{+}}/\tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^{M}\exp(h\cdot e_{f_{j}}/\tau)}, (2)

where f+f^{+} is the correct field label and τ\tau is a temperature hyperparameter. Only the LoRA adapters (Hu et al., 2022) on the attention projection matrices are updated; the pruned backbone itself remains frozen.

Semantic-Guided Feature Fusion.

After fine-tuning, we extract one embedding efe_{f} per field by encoding the field name and projecting the final hidden state of the model. Pairwise cosine similarities Si​jllmS^{\text{llm}}_{ij} between field embeddings are passed through a learnable transformation gθg_{\theta} to obtain task-adapted weights S~i​jllm\tilde{S}^{\text{llm}}_{ij}, which reweight the pairwise feature interactions of the CTR model:

Ci​jllm=S~i​jllm⋅Ii​jctr,C^{\text{llm}}_{ij}=\tilde{S}^{\text{llm}}_{ij}\cdot I^{\text{ctr}}_{ij}, (3)

where Ii​jctr=eictr⋅ejctrI^{\text{ctr}}_{ij}=e^{\text{ctr}}_{i}\cdot e^{\text{ctr}}_{j} denotes the pairwise CTR feature interaction. These reweighted interactions are aggregated into a contextual prediction stream ycontext=∑i<jCi​jllmy_{\text{context}}=\sum_{i<j}C^{\text{llm}}_{ij}, then combined with the interaction stream of the CTR model. During training, a KL-divergence additionally aligns the pairwise similarity distributions induced by the CTR and LLM embedding spaces. The overall loss combines prediction and alignment, ℒ=ℒBCE+λalign​ℒalign\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}}+\lambda_{\text{align}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}, where ℒBCE\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} is the binary cross-entropy loss for click prediction. At inference time, the pruned backbone is deployed directly, enabling online LLM-based semantic modeling without pre-caching.

3 Experiments

We evaluate SlimFM on four public CTR datasets: Amazon Gift Cards, Amazon Video Games, Amazon Digital Music, and MovieLens-1M, as shown in Table 1. We use six CTR backbones: FM (Rendle, 2010), DeepFM (Guo et al., 2017), FwFM (Pan et al., 2018), FmFM (Sun et al., 2021), FinalMLP (Mao et al., 2023), and Wukong (Zhang et al., 2024). We compare against LLM-enhanced baselines KAR (Xi et al., 2024), LLM-CF (Sun et al., 2024), CTRL (Li et al., 2023), and EASE (Qiu et al., 2024), all using the same LLaMA3-8B backbone for a fair comparison, plus two PLM-enhanced baselines, CELA (Wang et al., 2024) and ClickPrompt (Lin et al., 2024).

Efficiency. Table 2 reports parameters, multiply-accumulate operations (MACs), and single-sample inference latency (averaged over 50 runs with 10 warmup runs) across all six CTR backbones. The pruned backbone of SlimFM comprises 4504M parameters, substantially fewer than KAR (8032M) and LLM-CF (7075M), representing a 1.8×1.8\times reduction. This compression translates directly into lower inference latency: SlimFM consistently achieves 15.98–17.58 ms per prediction, versus 54.62–55.08 ms for KAR and 46.46–47.53 ms for LLM-CF, a 3.13.1–3.4×3.4\times speedup over KAR and 2.72.7–2.9×2.9\times over LLM-CF that holds across all six backbones. The near-invariance of per-method latency to CTR backbone choice confirms that the LLM forward pass is the inference bottleneck; structured pruning of the LLM is therefore the critical factor for reducing end-to-end inference latency.

Accuracy. Table 3 compares SlimFM against traditional CTR models, PLM-enhanced methods, and LLM-enhanced methods across all six backbones and four datasets. Averaged over the six backbones, SlimFM improves AUC relative to the base CTR model of each backbone by 1.69% on Gift Cards, 1.36% on Video Games, 1.39% on Digital Music, and 0.13% on MovieLens-1M. Notable combinations include Wukong on Gift Cards (AUC 0.6808, +4.63%) and FinalMLP on Gift Cards (0.6792, +4.19%), both the highest AUC among LLM-enhanced methods in their respective backbone group; FwFM achieves the largest gain on Video Games (AUC 0.6774, +5.41%); and DeepFM the strongest improvement on Digital Music (AUC 0.7686, +4.03%). Overall, SlimFM achieves the highest AUC among KAR, LLM-CF, CTRL, and EASE in 10 of the 24 backbone/dataset combinations; its RelaImpr remains positive across all datasets despite a 44% smaller LLM backbone than the uncompressed baselines.

Sparsity-performance trade-off. Table 4 reports accuracy across pruning levels for the FM backbone, ranging from 8B model (mean AUC 0.7346) to 2B parameters. Pruning to 6B retains 99.88% of the mean AUC, and pruning to 4.5B retains 99.77% while achieving roughly 1.8×1.8\times compression; only at the more aggressive 2B setting does the recovery rate drop further, to 99.62%, with the decline most visible on Gift Cards and Video Games. The compression trade-off is smooth and monotone, with no sharp degradation point, indicating that the 4.5B configuration offers a favorable balance between model compression and predictive accuracy.

4 Conclusion

We show that dependency-aware structured pruning of LLaMA3-8B, combined with field-aware fine-tuning and semantic-guided fusion, enables online LLM-based semantic modeling within a latency-critical CTR pipeline while retaining over 99% of full-model accuracy. These results demonstrate that structured pruning is not merely an optimization but a necessary mechanism for practical LLM-enhanced CTR deployment. Our evaluation is restricted to four CTR datasets and a single LLM family (LLaMA3-8B), so generalization to other backbones, domains, and LLM architectures remains to be verified.
